title: No. 81 — The Judiciary Continued, and the Distribution of the Judicial Authority. (Hamilton)
paragraphs: Let us now return to the division of judicial authority among different courts, and their relations to each other.

"The judicial power of the United States is" (by the plan of the Convention) "to be vested in one Supreme Court, and in such inferior courts as the Congress may, from time to time, ordain and establish."(1)

That there ought to be one court of supreme and final jurisdiction is a proposition not likely to be contested. The reasons for it have been given elsewhere and are too obvious to need repeating. The only question that seems to have been raised about it is whether it ought to be a distinct body or a branch of the legislature. Here we see the same contradiction that has been noticed in several other cases. The very men who object to the Senate as a court of impeachments, on the ground of an improper mixing of powers, argue, by implication at least, that the final decision of all causes should be vested in the whole or a part of the legislative body.

The arguments, or rather suggestions, on which this charge is founded run to this effect: "The authority of the proposed Supreme Court of the United States, which is to be a separate and independent body, will be superior to that of the legislature. The power of construing the laws according to the spirit of the Constitution will enable that court to mould them into whatever shape it may think proper; especially as its decisions will not be in any manner subject to the revision or correction of the legislative body. This is as unprecedented as it is dangerous. In Britain, the judicial power, in the last resort, resides in the House of Lords, which is a branch of the legislature; and this part of the British government has been imitated in the State constitutions in general. The Parliament of Great Britain, and the legislatures of the several States, can at any time rectify, by law, the exceptionable decisions of their respective courts. But the errors and usurpations of the Supreme Court of the United States will be uncontrollable and remediless." On examination, this will be found to consist entirely of false reasoning from a misunderstood fact.

In the first place, there is not a syllable in the plan under consideration that directly empowers the national courts to construe the laws according to the spirit of the Constitution, or that gives them any greater latitude in this respect than the courts of every State can claim. I admit, however, that the Constitution ought to be the standard for construing the laws, and that wherever there is an evident conflict, the laws ought to give way to the Constitution. But this doctrine does not follow from anything peculiar to the plan of the Convention. It follows from the general theory of a limited Constitution, and as far as it is true, it applies equally to most, if not all, of the State governments. There can be no objection on this account, therefore, to the federal judiciary that would not also lie against the local courts in general, and that would not serve to condemn every constitution that tries to set bounds to legislative discretion.

But perhaps the force of the objection may be thought to lie in the particular organization of the Supreme Court: in its being made up of a distinct body of judges, instead of being a branch of the legislature, as in the government of Great Britain and that of this State. To insist on this point, the authors of the objection must give up the meaning they have labored to attach to the celebrated maxim requiring a separation of the departments of power. Nevertheless, I will concede to them, in keeping with the interpretation given to that maxim in these papers, that it is not violated by vesting the ultimate power of judging in a PART of the legislative body. But though this is not an absolute violation of that excellent rule, it comes so close to one that on this account alone it is less desirable than the mode the Convention preferred. From a body that had even a partial hand in passing bad laws, we could rarely expect a disposition to temper and moderate them in application. The same spirit that had acted in making them would be too apt to act in interpreting them; and still less could we expect men who had infringed the Constitution as legislators to be disposed to repair the breach as judges. Nor is this all. Every reason that recommends the tenure of good behavior for judicial offices argues against placing the judicial power, in the last resort, in a body of men chosen for a limited period. It is absurd to refer the determination of causes in the first instance to judges of permanent standing and in the last instance to judges of a temporary and changing makeup. It is more absurd still to subject the decisions of men selected for their knowledge of the laws, acquired by long and laborious study, to the revision and control of men who, lacking the same advantage, cannot but be deficient in that knowledge. The members of the legislature will rarely be chosen with a view to the qualifications that fit men to be judges. So, just as there will be great reason to fear all the ill consequences of defective information, there will be no less reason, from the natural tendency of such bodies to divide into parties, to fear that the pestilential breath of faction may poison the fountains of justice. The habit of being continually marshaled on opposite sides will be too apt to stifle the voice both of law and of equity.

These considerations teach us to applaud the wisdom of those States that have committed the judicial power, in the last resort, not to a part of the legislature but to distinct and independent bodies of men. Contrary to the supposition of those who have described the plan of the Convention in this respect as novel and unprecedented, it is only a copy of the constitutions of New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia. The preference given to those models deserves high praise.

In the second place, it is not true that the Parliament of Great Britain, or the legislatures of the individual States, can rectify the exceptionable decisions of their respective courts in any sense other than one in which a future legislature of the United States could do the same. Neither the British constitution nor the State constitutions in theory authorizes a legislative act to revise a judicial sentence. Nor is there anything in the proposed Constitution, any more than in either of them, that forbids it. In the former as well as the latter, the sole obstacle is the impropriety of the thing on the general principles of law and reason. A legislature, without exceeding its province, cannot reverse a determination once made in a particular case, though it may prescribe a new rule for future cases. This is the principle, and it applies, with all its consequences, in exactly the same manner and extent to the State governments as to the national government now under consideration. Not the least difference can be pointed out in any view of the subject.

It may finally be observed that the supposed danger of judicial encroachments on the legislative authority, which has been repeated on many occasions, is in reality a phantom. Particular misconstructions and contraventions of the will of the legislature may now and then happen, but they can never be so extensive as to amount to a problem, or in any noticeable degree to affect the order of the political system. This may be inferred with certainty from the general nature of the judicial power, from the objects to which it relates, from the manner in which it is exercised, from its comparative weakness, and from its total incapacity to support its usurpations by force. And the inference is greatly strengthened by considering the important constitutional check that the legislative body would have over the members of the judicial department, through the power of instituting impeachments in one part of it and of deciding on them in the other. This alone is a complete security. There can never be danger that the judges, by a series of deliberate usurpations on the authority of the legislature, would risk the united resentment of the body entrusted with that authority, while that body had the means of punishing their presumption by removing them from their stations. While this ought to remove all apprehensions on the subject, it also supplies a cogent argument for making the Senate a court for the trial of impeachments.

Having now examined, and, I trust, removed the objections to the distinct and independent organization of the Supreme Court, I proceed to consider whether it is proper to have the power of constituting inferior courts,(2) and what relations will exist between these and the Supreme Court.

The power of constituting inferior courts is plainly meant to spare us from having to resort to the Supreme Court in every case of federal jurisdiction. It is intended to enable the national government to institute or authorize, in each State or district of the United States, a court competent to decide matters of national jurisdiction within its limits.

But why, it is asked, could the same purpose not have been accomplished through the State courts? This admits of different answers. Even if the fitness and competence of those courts is allowed in the fullest measure, the substance of the power in question may still be regarded as a necessary part of the plan, if only to empower the national legislature to commit to them the jurisdiction of causes arising out of the national Constitution. To confer the power of deciding such causes on the existing courts of the individual States would perhaps be as much "to constitute tribunals" as to create new courts with the same power. But ought not a more direct and explicit provision to have been made in favor of the State courts? There are, in my opinion, substantial reasons against such a provision. The most discerning cannot foresee how far a local spirit may prevail and disqualify the local courts for jurisdiction over national causes; while everyone can see that courts constituted like those of some of the States would be improper channels for the judicial authority of the Union. State judges who hold their offices at pleasure, or from year to year, will be too little independent to be relied on for an inflexible execution of the national laws. And if it were necessary to entrust original jurisdiction over causes arising under those laws to them, it would be equally necessary to leave the door of appeal as wide as possible. The ease or difficulty of appeals ought to be proportioned to the grounds for confidence or distrust in the subordinate courts. I am well satisfied that the appellate jurisdiction is proper in the separate classes of causes to which the plan of the Convention extends it. Still, I should consider anything calculated to give appeals an unrestrained course in practice as a source of public and private problems.

I am not sure that it will not prove highly expedient and useful to divide the United States into four, five or half a dozen districts, and to institute a federal court in each district, in place of one in every State. The judges of these courts, with the aid of the State judges, may hold circuits for the trial of causes in the separate parts of their respective districts. Through them justice may be administered with ease and dispatch, and appeals may safely be confined within a narrow compass. This plan appears to me at present the best of any that could be adopted; and for it to be possible, the power of constituting inferior courts must exist in the full extent in which it is found in the proposed Constitution.

These reasons should satisfy any open mind that lacking such a power would have been a serious defect in the plan. Let us now see how the judicial authority is to be divided between the supreme and inferior courts of the Union.

The Supreme Court is to have original jurisdiction only "in cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls, and those in which A STATE shall be a party." Public ministers of every class are the immediate representatives of their sovereigns. All questions in which they are concerned are so directly connected with the public peace that, both to preserve it and out of respect to the sovereignties they represent, it is expedient and proper for such questions to be submitted in the first instance to the highest court of the nation. Consuls do not strictly have a diplomatic character, but since they are the public agents of the nations to which they belong, the same observation applies to them in great measure. In cases in which a State might be a party, it would ill suit its dignity to be turned over to an inferior court.

This may be something of a digression from the subject of this paper, but I will take the occasion to mention a supposition that has caused some alarm on very mistaken grounds. It has been suggested that if the public securities of one State were assigned to the citizens of another, those citizens could sue that State in the federal courts for the amount of the securities. The following considerations prove this suggestion to be without foundation.

It is inherent in the nature of sovereignty not to be subject to suit by an individual without its consent. This is the general sense and the general practice of mankind, and the exemption, as one of the attributes of sovereignty, is now enjoyed by the government of every State in the Union. Unless the plan of the Convention surrenders this immunity, therefore, it will remain with the States, and the danger suggested must be merely imaginary. The circumstances necessary to bring about a transfer of State sovereignty were discussed in considering the article on taxation and need not be repeated here. Returning to the principles established there will satisfy us that there is no color for pretending that the State governments would, by adopting that plan, lose the privilege of paying their own debts in their own way, free from every constraint except that which flows from the obligations of good faith. Contracts between a nation and individuals are binding only on the conscience of the sovereign, and have no pretensions to compulsive force. They confer no right of action independent of the sovereign will. What would be the point of authorizing suits against States for the debts they owe? How could recoveries be enforced? Clearly it could not be done without waging war against the contracting State. To ascribe to the federal courts, by mere implication and in destruction of a pre-existing right of the State governments, a power that would involve such a consequence would be altogether forced and unwarrantable.

Let us pick up the thread again. We have seen that the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court would be limited to two kinds of causes, and those of a kind that seldom occur. In every other case of federal jurisdiction, original jurisdiction would belong to the inferior courts, and the Supreme Court would have only appellate jurisdiction, "with such exceptions and under such regulations as the Congress shall make."

Hardly anyone has questioned the propriety of this appellate jurisdiction in matters of law, but loud clamors have been raised against it in matters of fact. Some well-intentioned men in this State, taking their notions from the language and forms of our own courts, have come to see it as an implied replacement of trial by jury with the civil-law mode of trial used in our courts of admiralty, probate and chancery. They give the term "appellate" a technical sense, because in our legal usage it generally refers to appeals in the civil-law course. But if I am rightly informed, it would not carry that meaning anywhere in New England. There an appeal from one jury to another is familiar in both language and practice, and is even automatic until there have been two verdicts on one side. So the word "appellate" will not be understood the same way in New England as in New York, which shows how wrong it is to adopt a technical reading drawn from the law of any one State. Taken in the abstract, the expression means no more than the power of one court to review the proceedings of another, on the law or the fact or both. How it is done may depend on ancient custom or legislative provision (in a new government it must depend on the latter), and it may be done with or without a jury, as is thought advisable. If, therefore, the Constitution should in any case permit a fact once determined by a jury to be re-examined, it may be regulated so that a second jury does it, either by sending the cause back to the court below for a second trial of the fact, or by directing an issue straight out of the Supreme Court.

But it does not follow that the Supreme Court will be permitted to re-examine a fact once established by a jury. Why may it not be said, with the strictest propriety, when a writ of error is brought from an inferior to a superior court of law in this State, that the latter has jurisdiction of the fact as well as the law? It is true that it cannot begin a new inquiry into the fact, but it takes notice of the fact as it appears on the record and pronounces the law arising from it.(3) This is jurisdiction of both fact and law, and it is not even possible to separate them. Though the common-law courts of this State establish disputed facts by a jury, they undoubtedly have jurisdiction of both fact and law. Accordingly, when the facts are agreed on in the pleadings, they do not resort to a jury but proceed at once to judgment. On this ground, therefore, I contend that the expressions "appellate jurisdiction, both as to law and fact" do not necessarily imply a re-examination in the Supreme Court of facts decided by juries in the inferior courts.

We may well imagine that the following train of thought influenced the Convention in framing this particular provision. The appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (it may have been argued) will extend to causes decided in different modes, some in the course of the COMMON LAW, others in the course of the CIVIL LAW. In the former, generally speaking, the proper province of the Supreme Court will be to revise only the law. In the latter, re-examination of the fact is customary, and in some cases, of which prize causes are an example, might be essential to preserving the public peace. It is therefore necessary that the appellate jurisdiction should, in certain cases, extend in the broadest sense to matters of fact. It will not do to make an express exception of cases that were originally tried by a jury, because in the courts of some of the States all causes are tried in this mode(4), and such an exception would preclude the revision of matters of fact where it might be proper as well as where it might be improper. To avoid all problems, it will be safest to declare in general terms that the Supreme Court shall have appellate jurisdiction both as to law and fact, and that this jurisdiction shall be subject to such exceptions and regulations as the national legislature may prescribe. This will enable the government to shape it in the manner that will best serve the ends of public justice and security.

This view of the matter, at any rate, puts it beyond all doubt that the supposed abolition of trial by jury through this provision is false and untrue. The legislature of the United States would certainly have full power to provide that in appeals to the Supreme Court there should be no re-examination of facts that had been tried by juries in the original causes. This would certainly be an authorized exception. If, for the reason I have already suggested, it should be thought too broad, it might be qualified by confining it to those causes only that are decided at common law by that mode of trial.

The sum of the observations made so far on the authority of the judicial department is this. It has been carefully restricted to those causes that are plainly proper for the jurisdiction of the national judiciary. In the division of this authority, a very small portion of original jurisdiction has been kept for the Supreme Court and the rest assigned to the subordinate courts. The Supreme Court will have appellate jurisdiction, both as to law and fact, in all the cases referred to it, subject in both respects to any exceptions and regulations that may be thought advisable. This appellate jurisdiction in no case abolishes trial by jury. And an ordinary degree of prudence and integrity in the national councils will secure for us solid advantages from the establishment of the proposed judiciary, without exposing us to any of the problems that have been predicted from that source.
1. Article 3, Sec. 1.

2. This power has been absurdly represented as intended to abolish all the county courts in the individual States, which are commonly called inferior courts. But the expressions of the Constitution are, to constitute "tribunals INFERIOR TO THE SUPREME COURT"; and the evident design of the provision is to enable the institution of local courts, subordinate to the Supreme, either in States or larger districts. It is ridiculous to imagine that county courts were in contemplation.
3. This word is composed of JUS and DICTIO, juris dictio or a speaking and pronouncing of the law.
4. I hold that the States will have concurrent jurisdiction with the subordinate federal courts in many cases of federal jurisdiction, as will be explained in my next paper.
